conflict_topics: strong-smelling cooking (e.g. curry) in the shared kitchen
shared kitchen use vs. restricting certain foods
laundry contamination and drying logistics in the service yard
who has authority to set house rules / decide what counts as 'strong' smell
dialogue_quality_notes: Natural, concise turns reflecting practical concerns (e.g., A: 'I have to work from home at this table. The smell is a problem for my video calls.').
Participants offer concrete trade-offs and logistics (B's 'heads-up' proposal), not just slogans.
Some repeating of core points (smell spreads, laundry affected) but not excessive redundancy.
Consistent grounding in the shared physical constraints (kitchen, service yard, landlord rule).
evaluation.final_reason: No mutual agreement was reached. Agent A requested that nobody cook strong-smelling food. Agent D defended using the shared kitchen ('This is a shared kitchen. All of us use it to cook.'; 'All cooking has a smell.') and framed restrictions as asking them to stop cooking ('So I should stop cooking my own food?'). A proposed compromise (heads-up before cooking so laundry can be brought in) was offered by Agent B ('give a heads-up before cooking something strong; then people can bring their laundry in.'), but C and D pointed out a practical barrier: wet laundry cannot be accommodated in rooms ('It won't dry in my room...'; 'There's nowhere for wet laundry to go.'). There is no evidence that any party accepted a concrete arrangement, conceded their main demand, or committed to a changed behavior; the outstanding incompatibility therefore remains unresolved.
position_change_notes: No party conceded their core position during the run. Agent D acknowledged the smell spreads ('She's right. The smell goes everywhere.') but did not accept limiting their cooking.
Agent B moved toward proposing a practical compromise (heads-up; put laundry in rooms) but this was not accepted by C and later D due to dampness concerns.
Agent C consistently highlighted the laundry problem and rejected the proposed mitigation ('It won't dry in my room. It'll just make the room damp.').
Agent A consistently pressed for restriction of 'strong' smells and clarified what was meant, but did not secure agreement or an enacted rule.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: Agent A states a problem for work-from-home calls. Turn 2: Agent B agrees the smell is a problem. No opposing claims or demands yet.

Turn 3: Agent C notes laundry smells. Turn 4: Agent D responds 'This is a shared kitchen. All of us use it to cook.' This asserts a competing right/practice against the implicit request to restrict cooking smells.
Turn 5: Agent A clarifies the smell reaches the shared living room. Turn 6: Agent D counters 'All cooking has a smell.' Continued clear disagreement over whether cooking should be restricted.

Turn 7: Agent A distinguishes severity ('not all cooking smells fill the whole flat for hours'). Turn 8: Agent B offers opening windows/door as mitigation. The parties are still at odds; a partial mitigation is proposed but not accepted.
Turn 9: Agent C warns laundry would be affected. Turn 10: Agent D concedes smell spreads but frames it as inevitable ('That's just how the kitchen is.'). No concession on changing cooking.
Turn 11: Agent A: 'The kitchen doesn't change. What we cook in it does.' Turn 12: Agent D reacts defensively: 'So I should stop cooking my own food?' The dispute becomes more personal and entrenched.

Turn 13: Agent A narrows the request to 'any food with a smell that strong.' Turn 14: Agent B suggests closing a bedroom door and opening a window. The round contains a clarifying request and a proposed workaround but the core incompatibility remains unresolved.

Turn 15: Agent C: 'The laundry is still out there.' Turn 16: Agent D: 'Exactly. The smell gets on everything in the common area.' This reinforces the practical impact and D's resistance to restrictions.

Turn 17: Agent A: 'So we shouldn't be making smells that get on everything.' Turn 18: Agent D: 'And who decides what's a 'strong' smell?' The parties dispute both the norm and who has authority to decide.

Turn 19: Agent A defines 'strong' ('fills the whole flat for hours. Like the curry last night'). Turn 20: Agent B proposes a practical compromise: 'give a heads-up before cooking something strong; then people can bring their laundry in.' A conciliatory proposal appears, but it is not accepted by all parties yet.

Turn 21: Agent C asks where wet laundry would go. Turn 22: Agent B suggests rooms ('In our own rooms, maybe?'). The proposed mitigation meets practical objections and the core incompatibility remains.

Turn 23: Agent C: 'It won't dry in my room. It'll just make the room damp.' Turn 24: Agent D: 'She's right. There's nowhere for wet laundry to go.' The logistical solution collapses, highlighting an enduring, strong disagreement over cooking restrictions versus practical constraints.

substantive_insights: Conflict hinges on an incompatibility between one person's regular cooking (twice-weekly curry) and others' use of shared airspace for work and drying laundry.
Physical constraints (single kitchen, service yard for laundry, landlord forbids modifications) limit feasible solutions.
A low-cost mitigation (heads-up so laundry can be brought inside) fails because there is no suitable indoor space to store wet laundry without causing dampness.
Disagreement involves both a normative question ('should we ban strong smells?') and a practical one ('where would laundry go?'), and the latter defeats the modest compromise proposed.
